title: Does generative AI save time at work?
gist: New FRED series from the Generative AI Adoption Tracker show US workplace AI use broadening from 28.2% of employed adults in Q3 2024 to 39.2% in Q2 2026, while the share of work hours actually assisted rose only 4.1% to 6.3% and self-reported hours saved only 1.6% to 2.2%. The gap between near-40% headcount adoption and roughly 2% of hours saved is the article's real signal: the aggregate productivity dividend is real, rising, and still very small.

insights.claim: The share of employed US adults who used generative AI for work in the prior week rose from 28.2% in Q3 2024 to 39.2% in Q2 2026, per the Generative Artificial Intelligence Adoption Tracker series in FRED.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Roughly 11 points of workplace penetration in seven quarters is a fast but not exponential ramp — a base case for seat-based AI software TAM growth rather than a step-change.
insights.quote: The share of employed adults who used generative AI for work in the past week grew from 28.2% in Q3 2024 to 39.2% by Q2 2026, indicating adoption is broadening.

insights.claim: The share of US work hours assisted by generative AI grew from 4.1% to 6.3% between Q3 2024 and Q2 2026, meaning that even among a workforce approaching 40% weekly usage, AI touches only a low-single-digit share of actual hours worked.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Adoption headlines massively overstate workflow penetration; the depth metric — hours assisted, not user counts — is the better leading indicator for AI compute demand and per-seat monetization.
insights.quote: The share of work hours assisted by generative AI grew from 4.1% to 6.3% over roughly the same stretch.
insights.locator: All three lines trend steadily upward

insights.claim: Growth in generative AI usage is being driven by two distinct forces simultaneously: new workers trying the tools for the first time, and existing users increasing their intensity of use.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Intensity growth among existing users is the stickier revenue driver — watch usage-based/token consumption metrics over net-new seat adds.
insights.quote: More workers are trying generative AI, and the ones already using it are leaning on it more heavily.

themes.theme: The productivity dividend is real but tiny

insights.claim: Self-reported work hours saved thanks to generative AI assistance grew from 1.6% to 2.2% of total work hours between Q3 2024 and Q2 2026 — a level the FRED Blog flags as the most important of the three series.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A ~2% economy-wide time saving is meaningful at scale but far below the labor-displacement narratives priced into AI equities; it argues for a slow-burn productivity story, not an imminent headcount shock.
insights.quote: Perhaps most importantly, the share of work hours saved thanks to AI assistance grew from 1.6% to 2.2%.

insights.claim: Time saved by generative AI remains roughly one-third of the hours it assists — 2.2% saved against 6.3% assisted in Q2 2026, versus 1.6% against 4.1% in Q3 2024 — so the efficiency yield per assisted hour has not improved as adoption scaled.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Better models have so far bought more usage, not more savings per hour used; a break upward in that ratio would be the genuine signal that AI capability gains are converting into economics.
insights.locator: All three lines trend steadily upward

insights.claim: Rising measured time savings indicate generative AI has moved past being an experimental novelty and is beginning to free up genuine work hours.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Frames the debate away from 'is AI useful' toward 'how fast does the saved time convert into output or cost cuts' — the margin question for corporate earnings.
insights.quote: Rising time savings suggest AI is not just a novelty; it’s starting to free up real work hours.

insights.claim: If the current trend in adoption, hours assisted, and hours saved persists, generative AI could begin appearing in broad aggregate productivity statistics within the next several years.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Puts a multi-year, not multi-quarter, clock on the macro payoff — relevant to potential-GDP and neutral-rate assumptions rather than to next-quarter earnings.
insights.quote: If this trend holds, generative AI could show up in broader productivity statistics in the years ahead.

insights.claim: The 'time saved' figures in the AI adoption tracker are respondent self-reports, making the measurements inherently approximate rather than observed productivity data.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Discount the level but trust the direction: the series is best used as a trend/second-derivative indicator, and firm-level or task-level studies are needed to confirm the magnitude.
insights.quote: The information is based on how respondents self-report their “time saved,” so the measurements are inherently approximate.

insights.claim: The three series — weekly work use, hours assisted, and hours saved — are argued to be credible collectively because they move together in a mutually consistent pattern even though each is individually noisy.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A triangulation template for reading any self-reported AI-impact survey: require corroboration across breadth, depth, and outcome metrics before acting on a single headline number.
insights.quote: these three data series together do tell a coherent story of AI adoption

insights.claim: The Generative Artificial Intelligence Adoption Tracker was built by economists Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, and David Deming using the Real-Time Population Survey, a nationally representative online survey of working-age adults aged 18 to 64.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: A nationally representative, quarterly, free FRED series is the closest thing to an official high-frequency AI-diffusion gauge — usable as a repeatable input to macro and AI-exposure models.

insights.claim: The Real-Time Population Survey asks employed respondents each quarter how fast and how intensely they are adopting AI both at work and outside of work, giving a quarterly cadence to AI diffusion data.
insights.speaker: St. Louis Fed — FRED Blog
insights.so_what: Quarterly refresh means the series can be tracked as a recurring catalyst for the AI-productivity debate, unlike one-off academic studies.
insights.quote: Each quarter, employed respondents report how fast and how intensely they’re adopting AI technology both at work and outside of work.
